etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English residence, from Old French residence, from Medieval Latin residentia, from residēns, present participle of resideō, equivalent to reside +‎ -ence.

definitions.definition: The place where one lives (resides); one's home.

quote.citation: 1856 December, [Thomas Babington] Macaulay, “Samuel Johnson”, in T[homas] F[lower] E[llis], editor, The Miscellaneous Writings and Speeches of Lord Macaulay, new edition, London: Longman, Green, Reader, & Dyer, published 1871, →OCLC:
quote.text: Johnson took up his residence in London.

definitions.definition: A building or portion thereof used as a home, such as a house or an apartment therein.
The place where a corporation is established.
The state of living in a particular place or environment.

quote.citation: 1713, The History of the Common Law of England, Sir Matthew Hale (jurist), Google Books, page 87
quote.text: The confessor had often made considerable residences in Normandy.

definitions.definition: Accommodation for students at a university or college.
The place where anything rests permanently.

quote.citation: 1649, J[ohn] Milton, ΕΙΚΟΝΟΚΛΆΣΤΗΣ [Eikonoklástēs] […], London:  […]  Matthew Simmons, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: But when a king sets himself to bandy against the highest court and residence of all his regal power, he then  […]  fights against his own majesty and kingship.

quote.citation: 1627 (indicated as 1626), Francis [Bacon], “(please specify the page, or |century=I to X)”, in Sylua Syluarum: Or A Naturall Historie. In Ten Centuries. […], London:  […]  William Rawley […]; [p]rinted by J[ohn] H[aviland] for William Lee […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Separation […] is wrought by Weight; as in the ordinary Residence or Settlement of Liquors.

definitions.definition: That which falls to the bottom of liquors; sediment; also, refuse; residuum.
